body.text: This is what happened. In the early hours of Saturday 28 March 1953, Jean Cullen returned home to her flat at 274 Campbell Parade, North Bondi, having spent the evening visiting a friend in Rose Bay. She found two pieces of scrap paper and used one to write a note to her husband. This she left on the table in the breakfast room. The other she attached to the front door of the flat. In the kitchen she closed the door, opened the oven, turned on the gas, put a pillow on the floor and lay down.

John (Jack) Dickinson, Jean’s husband, had been spending the night with his mother at Woollahra. Arriving home at about 9.50 the next morning he found Jean’s key in the lock, and the note on the door, written in all caps: “Please don’t light a match. There is a gas leakage!” In the kitchen he turned off the gas and found Jean dead on the floor.

With the flat full of gas, Jack must have stumbled straight out and banged on a neighbour’s door. They called a local doctor and the police. Later, he found the other note Jean had left him. “No sad songs for me,” she began. She then listed details of her life insurance with AMP and superannuation with T&G Colonial Mutual and concluded: “It’s all yours Jack — if you take care of Spotty and Rusty. I believe you will because you are kind and I love you. Bye now.”

As a postscript she added that she had £280 in cash with the Commonwealth Bank and she wanted £100 of that to go to John’s mother — “please do that for me.” Over the page in all caps she wrote: “please have a whoop-it-up party.”

At the coronial inquest on 4 May there was no mention of Spotty and Rusty (dogs presumably), but Jean’s other careful arrangements suggest they were safe somewhere. Her Rose Bay friend was a Mrs Madeline Bray, resident manager of the Cranbrook Private Hotel in New South Head Road. She told the inquest that Jean had arrived at the hotel at about 9.45 on the evening before her death intending to stay the night, but after midnight had suddenly changed her mind and gone home. The pair had had a few glasses of rum but had not argued and Jean appeared to be sober. She was in good health according to Mrs Bray and had not mentioned that she was likely to take her own life.

Jack also said that Jean had never expressed such a wish. “She was quite happy,” he told the inquest. About a year before, however, she had a “small growth” removed from her right breast. She suffered no ill-effects from that, he said, and was in her “usual good health.” The coroner found that Clarice Jean Dickinson (Jean’s married name) had died from poisoning by carbon monoxide “wilfully caused by gassing herself at a gas oven.” There were no children.

Jean’s death at the age of thirty-two cut short a most successful career as an illustrator, cartoonist and comic strip artist. One of her many creations was “Pam,” a weekly comic strip about a pretty, exuberant teenaged girl syndicated across several capital city newspapers. A Pam strip appeared in the Adelaide Mail on the morning of Jean’s death. Pam’s young followers must have been disappointed at the sudden disappearance of their sassy heroine but they were probably unaware of the passing of her creator. There was some brief media coverage but the suicide was not mentioned — Jean had died “suddenly” at her flat, readers were told. That was all.

Jean had been one of a handful of women in Australia to achieve sustained success as a professional black-and-white artist. Even now the number of professional women cartoonists in Australia can’t be described as much more than a handful. I’m not going to speculate on the reasons because I have no idea. I’m not a cartoonist. I’m just going to tell the story of this one woman who died young and who is barely remembered now in the history of cartooning.
Maybe it will tell us something about women and cartooning, or even about women and work; maybe not. Maybe it’s just a story.

There is little to be known about the life of Jean Cullen outside her published artwork. If she was a letter-writer or a diary keeper, none of that appears to have survived, but in any case her absorbing passion was drawing. Given the hectic pace of her life, she probably had little time for anything else.

But let’s work with what we have because there are some small clues to her early life and character. She was born in Sydney in 1921 and although her parents were not well-off they seem to have managed their lives with some determination. Her father Clarence supported the family with a series of blue-collar jobs (storeman, wharf labourer, cabman) but was struck by a lorry and suffered a fractured thigh when Jean was six. Such an injury could have destroyed a family reliant on wages from manual labour, and in the ensuing years the Cullens do seem to have moved restlessly around Randwick, Manly and Coogee. Somehow they held things together, possibly helped by the fact that Jean was an only child.

About Jean herself, I discovered that she loved swimming. At age nine she was recorded sprinting thirty-three yards (thirty metres) in twenty-three seconds in a swim meet at the Domain baths, and at fourteen was still swimming competitively. Backstroke seems to have been her specialty. In 1936, aged fifteen, two of her drawings were published by the Sydney Sun’s children’s page. Both are beach scenes and this one shows early signs of her mature illustrative style. So, three things might be inferred: she was fast, she could draw, and she loved the beach.

In 1935 and 1936 Jean attended the prestigious National Art School at East Sydney Technical College, Darlinghurst. The annual fee of fifteen pounds was possibly as much as double Clarence Cullen’s weekly wage, but the sacrifice paid off. By the late 1930s Jean was working at Angus & Robertson, Australia’s most prestigious publishing house. Most of her assignments would have been unsigned illustration and graphic design work but she did get the opportunity to illustrate a couple of books of humorous verse: It’s ’Ard to Go Wrong in the Suburbs (1940), and It’s ’Ard to Keep Straight in the City (1941). Produced mainly to amuse troops away at the war, both went through seven or eight rapid printings.

A certain innocent sauciness in her work on the ’Ard books might have caught the attention of the editors of the Sydney paper, Smith’s Weekly, because by early 1942 she was working there as a staff cartoonist. Brash and boisterous, famous for its cartooning, Smith’s was probably much more fun to work for than dear old A&R.

Finding herself seated in the same art room in Smith’s Phillip Street building that had accommodated some of the most famous cartoonists of her day must have been extraordinary. Cec Hartt, George Finey, Virgil Reilly, and of course Stan Cross (creator of what was said to be Australia’s funniest cartoon) had all found fame at Smith’s but left by the time Jean started, and indeed the paper’s most successful years were behind it. Still, Jean worked alongside many prominent artists including Les Dixon, Joe Jonsson and Jim Russell.

Few photographs of her survive but one taken in late 1942, when she appeared in Smith’s “parade” of its artists, appears above. And this one, published by Smith’s, was taken on the day Jean and Jack got married in 1944. Jack is looking tenderly down at Jean while she obliges her photographer colleague with a bright smile for the camera. The paper was proud of its stable of cartoonists, paid them well and liked to promote them to readers.

Until it folded in 1950 Smith’s published hundreds of Jean’s cartoons (typically with her name or initials within the frame). She also produced elegant illustrations for a fashion column (the copy was probably written by Smith’s journalist Isla Brook) and had the occasional full-page spread of her own.

In a history of the paper published in 1966, long-time Smith’s journalist George Blaikie writes that its commitment to cartooning was unwavering from its inception in 1919, and that very quickly “it was the opinion of Fleet Street” that the paper had the “best team of black-and-white newspaper artists anywhere in the world.” So, if a cartoonist could make it at Smith’s Weekly, they could make it anywhere, and this was certainly true for Jean.

She survived its demise to be one of about ten artists and journalists selected by newspaper baron Keith Murdoch as part of a plan to launch a new national paper. According to Blaikie, Murdoch died before this ambition could be realised but the group kept going under George Blaikie’s editorship. For “rations and discipline” (as Blaikie, an ex-military man, put it) the unit was attached to Murdoch’s Brisbane Courier Mail but its content was syndicated across many capital city and regional newspapers. Jean’s work mainly appeared in the Adelaide Mail.

Now at last Jean could develop her own cartoon strip, and so her character Pam was born. Her generation had grown up reading Ginger Meggs and Bluey & Curley, but Pam was created for Australian adolescent girls. Pam’s first strip appeared on 3 February 1951.

Her fashion column continued, now entitled “Jean Cullen’s Clothes Horse” but with the copy properly credited to her colleague, Isla Brook, who had also joined the Blaikie venture. The column gave the two women an entree into some of Sydney’s glamorous fashion events.

Jean had reached the greatest success any Australian black-and-white artist could aspire to. For years she’d made a good living in a profession in which many try but most fall by the wayside. Her progress after she left art school feels like a joyful sashay from one career highlight to the next, and perhaps it was. And yet by early 1953, something had obviously gone very badly wrong.

Are cartoonists more prone to suicide than other people? Art historian Joan Kerr thought so, mentioning Jean’s death as an example. The sad clown of cartooning was “snappily summarised,” she writes, in a cartoon by Larry Burns published in the Australian Cartoonists’ Association magazine Inkspot in 1991: “My dad’s a cartoonist / Mine’s a miserable sod too.”

In Jean’s time, two terrible deaths loomed over Sydney’s artists’ community. First there was Smith’s cartoonist Joe Lynch, who drowned in 1927 after falling from a Sydney ferry, weighed down by bottles of beer in his coat pockets. He was on his way to Mosman to a party at the house of his Smith’s colleague, caricaturist George Finey. His body was never recovered, and whether his death was an accident or suicide no one knew, although many suspected suicide. Joe’s poet and journalist friend Kenneth Slessor brooded on Joe’s loss for years and slowly worked his dark meditations into his poem Five Bells, which was published in 1939 and became his most anthologised work.

Second was Cec Hartt, an Anzac wounded on Gallipoli whose cartoons helped make Smith’s the “Digger’s paper.” Any returned man who turned up at the paper’s office in search of a drink and a yarn found a friend in him. In May 1930 he drove to a remote spot near Moruya on the south coast of New South Wales and shot himself in the head. A funeral urn said to contain his ashes was kept on a shelf in the Smith’s art room.

No one published a lament or sounded any bells for Jean after she died. Perhaps that was what she wanted — “no sad songs for me.” There was not even an obituary unless you count a few discreet notices in the press. She died at home in her own kitchen, a commonplace and entirely predictable setting for a woman’s suicide, whereas the dark waters of Sydney Harbour heave with the kind of mystery and tragedy appropriate for that of a man. Five bells for Joe, none for Jean.

Something obviously drove her into a state of profound pain and isolation that could only be vanquished by death. What? The return of her breast cancer, if that’s what it was, seems the most obvious reason, although if so then she had apparently not shared the news with Jack, and the coroner sought no medical evidence. Still, Jean could have found the prospect of the painful and disfiguring treatment unendurable.

Depression and alcohol might also have been involved. The artists and journalists she mixed with lived alcohol-soaked lives. George Blaikie dubbed Smith’s staff the “hardest-drinking newspaper team in Australian, if not in Empire history,” and Jean was a regular at the Friday night “at homes” in the art room at Phillip Street, beer smuggled through from the Assembly Hotel next door.

And quite possibly, despite her success, the pressures of her job simply crushed her. It takes tremendous grit to cope with the deadlines, the demands (or indifference) of editors, and the need to be clever and funny all the time. Complex pre-arrangements must be made to take even the briefest holiday, and indeed there was no break in Jean’s output of Pam strips during her years with Blaikie’s unit. All cartoonists face these challenges but Jean and other women cartoonists carried an additional psychological burden. Just being a woman made the job much harder.

In 1929 Smith’s added two very young women to its cartooning staff, Mollie Horseman and Joan Morrison. Blaikie described Mollie as “tall, willowy, blonde and gay”; Joan as “dark, tiny, dainty and quiet.” Both were only aged about eighteen and had studied at the National Art School, which Jean would later attend. They were dubbed the “Smith sisters” and accommodated in an art room of their own with a notice on the door put there by the paper’s editor: “Keep Out.”

Both became well-known to readers, but in the early 1940s Mollie moved with her family to Queensland. Jean may never have worked with her although, in this close-knit community, they probably did meet. Joan was still there for most of Jean’s first year at Smith’s but then apparently went freelance. That left Jean as the only woman staff cartoonist on the paper.

All three women were obliged to cartoon like the men and produce work that conformed to the gender stereotyping that was all-pervasive in popular culture then, and for a long time to come. This was the standard of humour the Smith sisters’ editor thought readers would enjoy, and this is typical of the sort of thing Jean turned out probably every second week. And in such an aggressively male environment, who knows what other humiliations — or worse — they might have endured. (“C’mon love, surely you can take a joke?”)

When Virgil Reilly grew “weary” of the beautiful long-legged girls he’d been drawing for Smith’s since the 1920s — work that had made him one of the most highly paid newspaper artists in the country — the work went to Joan. “Virgil girls” thereafter became “Morrison girls” although Joan turned her into a “pretty little girl with a rounded figure and soft fluffy hair,” modelled on herself, Blaikie thought. (He failed to notice what Joan Kerr later picked up, that Morrison girls were independent beings: “powerful, funny, amoral, greedy and in control of most situations.”)

Jean’s way of dealing with the culture at Smith’s was to be quite uninhibited in the expression of her beauty and sexuality. Blaikie tells a story about her, a tall story needing a bit of lopping I think, that might actually contain a kernel of truth. Jean was “an attractive young creature,” he wrote, and during the Pacific war set herself the challenge of getting engaged to as many American servicemen of officer rank as she could at the one time. She did not take on multiple identities but always presented herself as Jean Cullen of Smith’s Weekly. To claim a “kill” she had to receive an engagement ring from the “victim.”

She would bring her latest fiancé to Smith’s Friday night parties where her colleagues (all in on the joke) got to know all seven of her future husbands. Of course the skill lay in remembering what she’d said to each man and ensuring no two of them were in Sydney at the same time. Her most admirable “capture” was an airforce general whose silver stars she had made into a brooch.

All this time her “true love” was a young Australian “Digger,” so the story went. As soon as he was home on leave they married, and Jean’s new husband (Jack, of course) joined the Friday night “dings” at Smith’s. Blaikie obviously relished portraying Jean as a man-eater, a temptress skilled at luring cashed-up, guileless American men into her web when all along a good, decent Aussie bloke was waiting to claim her.

Here’s another story, and this one really is true. In 1945 Jean wrote and illustrated a booklet entitled Hold that Halo, or How to Lose It in Ten Easy Lessons. It was published by a shortlived Sydney outfit called Allied Authors and Artists, which published mostly comics and cheap potboilers but also the work of more important authors like Frank Clune. In nonsense verse Jean advised girls who want to enjoy life that they should ditch their “halos” — referring, fairly obviously, to their virginity.

In Adelaide Hold that Halo was spotted and bought by detective Jacobus Vogelsang, the very same police officer who, the year before, had pursued Max Harris over the apparent indecency of the Ern Malley poems. As a result, the booklet’s distributor, Gordon & Gotch, was charged in the Adelaide Police Court with having sold an indecent publication. The magistrate found Halo immoral but not obscene and recorded a conviction without penalty. Gordon & Gotch was to pay costs.

Two of Jean’s drawings attracted particular comment. One showed the back of a couch with a woman’s arm flung above it. Was the couple on it merely kissing or…? The other showed a spinsterish-looking woman gazing intently at a row of library books with titles like “How to be Happy Though Not Married,” “The Secret of Sex,” and “Say Yes and Like It.”

In Sydney, Dymocks refused to carry the booklet but it sold briskly at other outlets. One newsagent in Darlinghurst was shifting 150 a day, and quite soon all stocks were gone. Jean herself was not involved in the legal proceedings and was quite unembarrassed about the whole affair. In a press interview she said she was amazed that something she’d written for a “lark” was taken so seriously. She’d first roughed out the idea when she was sixteen but had “toned it down” for publication. It’s not hard to imagine the roars of laughter over that at the next “ding” in the art room at Smith’s.

Last month I went to Bondi beach to see for myself where Jean had once lived. She’d moved there by 1943, her generous salary from Smith’s having enabled her to leave behind those sad old terrace houses she’d grown up in. Her parents appear to have moved with her but Clarence died that same year. Jack joined the household on his return from the war in 1945, but Jean’s mother Louisa (or Louise) died in 1951, leaving Jean and Jack with the apartment to themselves.

I knew from Google that her six-storey block on Campbell Parade — “La Pacifique” as it was known then and is now — is a superb example of Bondi’s art deco architecture. It’s one of a row of mostly original blocks probably dating from the late 1930s, many with exteriors painted in almost painfully cheerful colours. “La Pacifique” is sky-blue and “Sunray,” next door, is — naturally — bright yellow.

Alas I arrived to discover that “La Pacifique” is being renovated and its blueness is entirely greyed out by scaffolding. From a sign on the hoarding I learned that the building’s art deco lobbies, staircase, stained glass and ceilings are being restored, its services modernised and its façade renewed to withstand the coastal environment “for another fifty years.” This does at least confirm what I had suspected, that in choosing this as a place to live Jean had embraced modernity, luxury, style and all the energy and vitality of a highly urbanised, youthful beachside suburb.

With the “Pacifique” ocean at her door, this ought to have been an idyllic existence. Clearly not. In a disconsolate frame of mind I wandered up and down past the apartment block a few times, trying to unsee all that scaffolding, and then around to the rear of the building on Brighton Boulevard. Here, on the day of her death, a mortuary van must have quietly pulled up to take her remains to the city morgue.

I’d never been to Bondi beach before and have had little experience of beach culture. Obviously the precinct is more developed now, but there are still several grand hotels on Campbell Parade where she and Jack might have met friends for dining and dancing. The morning I was there the cafes, restaurants and ice creameries were bustling with young people: slim, tanned, fit and in pursuit of pleasure. Paddling in the shallows I walked the length of the beach from south to north, past the famous surf pavilion, watching the swimmers and surfers, and the lifesavers practicing their drills.

Suddenly three extraordinarily beautiful young women emerged from the surf, all of them nearly naked in micro-bikinis, skin glistening in the sun. Chatting among themselves they walked across the sand ahead of me, heedless of any eyes that might have been following them. They didn’t care, and why should they? I glanced up at “La Pacifique” and thought of how Jean might have enjoyed capturing the moment on paper. Here, surely, is the freedom she wanted for the young women of her time. •
